_about: PRO batch 45: era 4, The Veteran (34-37), set 3.

scenarios.title: The Missed Family Event
scenarios.text: Football makes you miss an important family occasion: {sibling}'s fortieth birthday, the one the whole family planned for a year, on the same night as a road game across the country.

choices.label: Call in during the toast
choices.result: A video call, propped against a glass at the head table, during the toasts. You make a speech from a hotel room and {sibling} laughs until they can't breathe.

choices.label: Plan your own celebration
choices.result: A second celebration, planned by you for the bye week: just the two of you, the old fishing spot, a cooler of sandwiches. {sibling} says it was better than the party.

choices.label: Send a gift and an apology
choices.result: A thoughtful gift and an honest apology, sent ahead of the party. {sibling} understands, and the photos you see the next morning sting more than you expected.

scenarios.title: The Investment Decision
scenarios.text: Your advisor brings a proposal: a large investment in your life after football, a training facility with your name on it, a business you'd run when your leg finally says no.

choices.label: Build the facility
choices.result: The facility, built over two years, with a kicking field and a gym and your name over the door. It's the biggest bet you've ever made, and it feels like a future.

choices.label: Start smaller
choices.result: Something smaller first: two clinics a summer, rented fields, a real waiting list. If it works, you'll build; if not, you'll have learned cheaply.

choices.label: Keep your money safe
choices.result: Safe, for now, where it is. Your advisor agrees, a little disappointed, and the idea stays on a napkin in your desk drawer.

scenarios.title: The Career Retrospective
scenarios.text: A respected journalist wants to tell the story of your whole career, start to finish, in a long magazine piece: your childhood, the bad years, the people who stayed.

choices.label: Tell all of it
choices.result: Everything, including the hardest parts, over six long interviews. The piece is beautiful and painful, and strangers write to you for months.

choices.label: Let the people around you talk
choices.result: The journalist, sent to {parent}, {holder} and your first coach instead. The story is about them as much as you, which is exactly right.

choices.label: Keep some things private
choices.result: Most of it, told; some of it, kept. The piece is good and careful, and you're glad of the parts that stayed yours.

scenarios.title: The Thirty-Fifth Birthday
scenarios.text: Another birthday in camp, and the young players bake you a cake shaped like a walker, with candles on the wheels and a card signed by the entire roster.

choices.label: Laugh harder than anyone
choices.result: The loudest laugh in the cafeteria is yours, and you blow out every candle on the walker. The photo ends up in the team's yearbook.

choices.label: Give a speech about getting old
choices.result: Standing on a cafeteria chair, you give a short speech about what getting old in this league actually teaches you. It starts as a joke and ends with the room silent.

choices.label: Get revenge in practice
choices.result: Revenge, served in practice: every rookie who signed the card has to shag your kicks for an hour. They do it laughing, and you kick beautifully.

scenarios.title: Training for Longevity
scenarios.text: You rebuild your whole training plan around recovery instead of volume: fewer kicks, more sleep, a pool, a massage therapist on speed dial. It feels like cheating.

choices.label: Commit to the new plan
choices.result: The new plan, followed exactly, for a whole season. Your leg feels five years younger by October, and you stop feeling guilty about the pool.

choices.label: Keep some of the old volume
choices.result: Half the new plan and half the old one. It's a compromise your body tolerates, and the trainers argue about it in meetings.

choices.label: Teach it to the young kickers
choices.result: The new plan, taught to the young kickers too, so they don't wait until their thirties. They think it's for old people, until their legs feel better.

scenarios.title: The Doctor's Honest Talk
scenarios.text: The team doctor closes the door and tells you, plainly, how much longer your hip has: two seasons, maybe three, if you're careful, and the word 'careful' is underlined.

choices.label: Plan the next two seasons around it
choices.result: Two seasons, planned carefully with the doctor and the trainers. Knowing the number, strangely, makes every kick feel more precious.

choices.label: Tell your family that night
choices.result: The number, told at the kitchen table that night. Nobody cries until the kids are asleep, and then everyone does, a little.

choices.label: Ignore the number
choices.result: Numbers are for other people, you tell yourself. You kick hard all season, and the doctor's underline stays in your head anyway.

scenarios.title: The Teammates Half Your Age
scenarios.text: Somewhere in the middle of a team meeting, you realize half your teammates were in middle school when you were drafted. One of them used to have your poster.

choices.label: Tell them about your draft day
choices.result: Your draft day, told at lunch: the motel, the phone, the cheap cake. The young players listen like it's an old movie.

choices.label: Ask about their middle school
choices.result: Their middle schools, their first teams, their old posters. You learn more about the room in an hour than in a whole season.

choices.label: Feel old, then kick
choices.result: A long moment of feeling very old, and then a very good practice. Age is a number, mostly, on good days.

scenarios.title: The New Coach Who Doesn't Know You
scenarios.text: A new head coach arrives from another conference. He has never seen you kick in person, and in his first meeting he calls you by the wrong name.

choices.label: Show him in practice
choices.result: No correction, just practice: the best week of kicks you've had all year. By Friday he knows your name and uses it twice.

choices.label: Introduce yourself properly
choices.result: Your name, said with a smile and a handshake after the meeting. He laughs, apologizes, and asks you to lunch to explain the specialists.

choices.label: Send him your film
choices.result: Three seasons of film, organized and labeled, left on his desk. He watches all of it that weekend and calls you on Sunday night.

scenarios.title: Three Possible Futures
scenarios.text: A retirement planner lays three futures on the table: retire now, retire in two years, or play until the body decides. Only one of them has football in it for long.

choices.label: Choose the two-year plan
choices.result: Two more years, planned in detail, with money set aside for the year after. It's the first time the end has felt like a place you can walk to.

choices.label: Take all three home
choices.result: All three futures, taken home and spread out on the dining table. Your family argues for a week and agrees on one.

choices.label: Keep playing and decide later
choices.result: Football, for as long as it lasts, and the planning later. The planner sighs and leaves the folder, just in case.

scenarios.title: The Teen at Home
scenarios.text: Your teenager stops coming to games. They say they're busy, and maybe they are, but their seat in the family section stays empty every Sunday.

choices.label: Ask them why, gently
choices.result: Why, asked gently on a long drive. It's not about you; it's about a friend, a fight, a life of their own. You listen, and they come to one game in December.

choices.label: Go to their thing instead
choices.result: Their thing, instead: a robotics competition on a Saturday, front row. They're surprised and proud, and they come to the next home game.

choices.label: Give them space
choices.result: Space, on purpose. The empty seat hurts, and you let it, and they come back on their own the next fall.

scenarios.title: The College Visits
scenarios.text: You drive your kid to college visits during the offseason: four campuses, three states, one minivan, a lot of arguments about the radio and one very nervous teenager.

choices.label: Let them lead every visit
choices.result: Every visit, led by them; you walk two steps behind. They pick the one with the best library, and you're secretly thrilled.

choices.label: Visit the athletic departments too
choices.result: The athletic departments, visited too, because you can't help it. Your kid rolls their eyes, and then asks a kicker on one team for a selfie.

choices.label: Make it a road trip
choices.result: Diners, a baseball game, a terrible motel with a pool shaped like a guitar: the trip becomes the thing they remember, much more than the campuses.

scenarios.title: The Last Contract Year
scenarios.text: This may be your last contract year. Your agent doesn't say it, the club doesn't say it, and everyone in your house is very careful not to say it either.

choices.label: Say it out loud
choices.result: Out loud, at dinner: this might be the last one. The silence breaks, everyone talks at once, and it's a relief.

choices.label: Make it count
choices.result: Every practice, every rep, every week, as if it's the last one. Your best season in three years, and the club notices.

choices.label: Plan both outcomes
choices.result: A plan for staying and a plan for stopping, both written down at the kitchen table. Whatever happens in March, everyone in the house is ready for it.

scenarios.title: The Long Goodbye of a Teammate
scenarios.text: A teammate's career is ending slowly: he's slower every week, hurt more often, and he won't admit any of it. The coaches have started talking around him.

choices.label: Talk to him honestly
choices.result: An honest talk, after practice, in the front seat of his truck. He gets angry, then quiet, then thanks you a week later in the weight room.

choices.label: Help him plan what's next
choices.result: A list of people he should call, coaches and broadcasters and business friends. When the end comes, he has somewhere to go.

choices.label: Let him find it himself
choices.result: His to find, you decide, and you just stay close. He announces it in December, and he calls you first.
